target.title: feat: add readiness conditions and providers
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, but readiness is evaluated by a fixed set of Gateway checks. Hosts and operators cannot select the additional criteria that define readiness for a deployment, plugins cannot contribute bounded observational evidence, and CLI, health, and status surfaces do not share one canonical result.

That leaves Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and other hosts maintaining private scripts to answer a basic question: is this OpenClaw instance ready to accept work under its configured requirements?

## Proposal

This draft implements the readiness portion of RFC 0018:

- normalize Gateway startup, admission, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, event-loop, configuration, plugin, and workspace evidence into structured conditions
- distinguish required conditions, which fail readiness on `False` or `Unknown`, from advisory conditions, which remain visible without changing the ready result
- let operators select built-in and plugin-contributed criteria directly with `gateway.readiness`
- let activated plugins register namespaced, self-describing criteria through the public plugin registry
- bound plugin checks with per-criterion timeouts, an overall readiness deadline, stable redacted timeout/error results, short caching, and in-flight coalescing that never duplicates a callback still pending after timeout
- return a required `ReadinessEvaluationComplete=Unknown` condition if canonical evaluation times out or fails, rather than hanging or rejecting health/status requests
- project the same canonical result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, Gateway `ready`, health, status, and `openclaw ready`
- provide human-readable and `--json` CLI output with fail-closed exit status

Example operator selection:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: ["openclaw.workspace-writable", "plugin.example.dependency"],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

Core selector IDs are configuration identities: selecting `openclaw.workspace-writable` emits the stable canonical `WorkspaceWritable` condition. Plugin criteria use their full namespaced ID as the condition type.

A plugin may contribute observational evidence without changing readiness by default:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "dependency",
  description: "Example dependency is reachable",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    const reachable = await probeDependency(pluginConfig, { signal });
    return reachable
      ? { status: "True", reason: "DependencyReachable", message: "Dependency is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "DependencyUnavailable", message: "Dependency is unavailable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes that registration as `plugin.<plugin-id>.dependency`. Operators explicitly select it in `requiredCriteria` when it belongs in their serving contract.

## Compatibility

Existing `/ready` and `/readyz` routes retain their HTTP contract: `200` when all required conditions are true and `503` otherwise. Existing installations need no readiness configuration. The universal Gateway lifecycle baseline always applies; explicitly selected criteria add deployment-specific evidence.

This PR does **not** add hosting profiles, profile selection, node-mode profiles, runtime activation identity, release conformance, Lobster concepts, tenant concepts, OCC resources, or policy/Doctor dependencies. Standard Hosting Profiles are separated into RFC 0023 so this readiness facility can stand on its own.

## Review Stack

This is one upstream PR with four commits. The fork PRs preserve the same smaller review boundaries:

- [PR 17: canonical Gateway readiness conditions](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17)
- [PR 22: workspace writability criterion](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22)
- [PR 23: selectable readiness providers](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23)
- [PR 27: canonical `openclaw ready` CLI](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27)

The implementation is rebased onto OpenClaw main `5fc7ba6da031`.

## Validation

- exact head: `89d8607aab9f9a942d45a6910cba1db3a210e239`
- all 19 changed test files pass in every selected Vitest project: 22 files/shards and 259 assertions
- Oxfmt passes on 59 changed TypeScript/JavaScript/Markdown files; Oxlint passes on 54 changed TypeScript/JavaScript files; `git diff --check` passes
- plugin SDK surface validation passes at the exact post-harvest budget: 328 public entrypoints and 10,615 public exports, with no forbidden package subpaths
- package build, public SDK declaration graph, package inventory, and tarball integrity checks pass
- final Codex review against current base reports no actionable correctness regression
- exact-head package-installed Docker proof passes with image `sha256:8add3c4f8ce2f1a444a735c43f19eac4ee0212778123fb883ff8f9f785a9fd0d`
- `/ready` and `/readyz` transition `200 -> 503 -> 200` when a required workspace is removed and restored; `/healthz` remains `200`; `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same `WorkspaceWritable / WorkspaceMissing` condition

`pnpm check:changed` is not claimed locally: this linked WSL worktree delegates that command to Blacksmith Testbox, and the local credential cannot access the `openclaw` organization. The changed-file tests and local static/package gates above passed; GitHub CI remains authoritative for repository-wide lanes.

## Published Upgrade Proof

The repository's `published-upgrade-survivor` Docker lane passed from the current published `openclaw@2026.7.1` package to a `2026.7.2` tarball carrying this four-commit readiness patch.

```text
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_PUBLISHED_BASELINE=1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_BASELINE_SPEC=openclaw@2026.7.1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_CANDIDATE=current \
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=16384 \
  bash scripts/e2e/upgrade-survivor-docker.sh
```

The lane installed and configured 2026.7.1 first, seeded agents, sessions, workspaces, credentials, channel/plugin settings, and legacy plugin dependency state, validated the baseline, upgraded the same installation through `openclaw update`, ran non-interactive Doctor and config validation, and revalidated preserved state before starting the candidate Gateway.

All 54 recorded phases passed on proved head `e5f5e97332e5495e65c1993dba258109849bdece`. Gateway startup took 47 seconds, `/healthz` 1 second, `/readyz` 1 second, and RPC status 2 seconds. The final head is a patch-equivalent rebase over seven later upstream commits; `git range-diff` shows the readiness commits unchanged except for the SDK export budget adapting to upstream's deletion. The exact final head then passed the package build, tarball integrity, and package-installed `200 -> 503 -> 200` runtime proof above.

Compatibility is explicit: the upgraded existing installation did not silently acquire `WorkspaceWritable` or another opt-in criterion as a new requirement. Its existing Gateway lifecycle baseline remained ready. An operator who explicitly requires workspace writability receives the intended fail-closed transition and matching CLI exit status.

target.title: fix(gateway): prune channel SecretRef surfaces before eager preflight while crash-loop breaker is tripped
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The persisted Gateway crash-loop breaker claims to enter a control-plane-safe mode that suppresses channel/provider account auto-start, but `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()` performs eager SecretRef preflight **before** the suppression reaches the channel manager. An unavailable channel credential continues to terminate the entire Gateway, and the supervisor keeps restarting it — defeating the safe-mode contract.

Root cause: `pruneSkippedStartupSecretSurfaces()` only checks `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` / `OPENCLAW_SKIP_PROVIDERS` env vars, ignoring the crash-loop breaker's `channelAutostartSuppression`. The breaker computes the suppression in `run.ts:beginBoot()` before calling `startGatewayServer()`, but the secrets activator resolves SecretRefs without knowing about it.

Additionally, the original fix (v1) passed the channel-pruned config as the snapshot's `sourceConfig`. On breaker startup this removed configured channels from the source, so a later credential repair and `secrets.reload` could not reconstruct channel assignments — violating the safe-mode contract that channel recovery should be possible without a Gateway restart.

Fixes #106379

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix carries the already-computed `channelAutostartSuppression` into the secrets activator and `prepareGatewayStartupConfig()`. The pruned config is now passed as `assignmentConfig` while the full config is kept as `sourceConfig`:

- **Startup**: channel surfaces are pruned from the assignment projection, preventing an unavailable channel SecretRef from blocking control-plane startup
- **Recovery**: the complete channel-bearing source config is preserved in the snapshot, so `secrets.reload` can resolve channel credentials after repair without a Gateway restart

Changes (v2 revision):
- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts`: pass full `config` + pruned `assignmentConfig` to `prepareSecretsRuntimeSnapshot` and `prepareSecretsRuntimeFastPathSnapshot`; simplify `canReusePreflightPreparedSnapshot` to compare full config directly
- `src/secrets/runtime-fast-path.ts`: add optional `assignmentConfig` parameter, using it for the resolved projection while source config remains complete for recovery
- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.secrets.test.ts`: 5 test cases updated to verify source/assignment projection separation — full source config preserves channels, assignment projection prunes them

## User Impact

- **Affected**: supervised Gateways (systemd, launchd) with an unavailable channel SecretRef where the persisted crash-loop breaker has tripped
- **Before**: Gateway keeps restarting; control plane unreachable
- **After**: breaker trips → channel surfaces pruned before SecretRef resolution → Gateway starts successfully → operator repairs credential → `secrets.reload` resolves the now-available credential from the preserved source config
- Normal startup behavior is unchanged; gateway auth and non-channel secrets remain fail-closed

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof: Breaker + secrets.reload Recovery (2026-07-14, revision v2)

**Setup**: `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-proof-revise/state`, config with gateway auth (password mode) + telegram channel referencing non-existent env var `NONEXISTENT_TG_BOT_TOKEN_106405`.

**Step 1 — Breaker simulation**: 3 unclean boot rows inserted into `gateway_boot_lifecycle`:
```
breaker-sim-1 | NULL    | NULL
breaker-sim-2 | NULL    | NULL  
breaker-sim-3 | startup_failed | NULL
```

**Step 2 — Gateway with breaker + bad channel**:
```
restart-loop breaker tripped: 3 unclean boot(s) within 300000ms;
  suppressing channel/provider account auto-start.
wrote stability bundle: .../openclaw-stability-...-gateway.crash_loop_breaker.json
...
http server listening (10 plugins...; 2.1s)
ready
```

Gateway reached `ready` with breaker tripped — bad channel SecretRef no longer blocks control-plane startup.

**Step 3 — Before reload: Telegram channel not loaded**:
```
$ openclaw gateway --password pw call channels.status --params '{"channel":"telegram"}' --json
{ "ok": false, "error": { "code": "INVALID_REQUEST", "message": "unknown channel: telegram" } }
```
Channel auto-start was suppressed by the breaker.

**Step 4 — secrets.reload after credential repair**:
```
$ export NONEXISTENT_TG_BOT_TOKEN_106405="proof-repaired-token"
$ openclaw gateway --password pw call secrets.reload --json
{ "ok": true, "warningCount": 0 }
```
`secrets.reload` succeeds — the full source config (preserved in the snapshot) allows the reload to resolve the now-available channel credential without errors.

**Result**: Gateway starts in safe mode with breaker tripped. `secrets.reload` can re-resolve credentials from the preserved source config — proving the source/assignment projection split preserves recovery state.

### Unit Test Evidence

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-startup-config.secrets.test.ts
 ✓ 26 tests passed (1 shard)
```

5 updated test cases verify source/assignment projection separation:
- breaker suppression active → source preserves channels, assignment prunes them
- breaker suppression null → regression guard (both preserve channels)
- breaker + gateway auth SecretRef → auth resolves, source preserves channels, assignment pruned
- `prepareGatewayStartupConfig` integration → channels pruned in assignment, preserved in source
- `OPENCLAW_SKIP_CHANNELS` env var → source preserves channels, assignment pruned

### Build & Checks

- `pnpm build` — passed
- `pnpm check:test-types` — passed
- `oxlint` — clean
- `pnpm format:check` — passed
- `git diff --check` — clean

### Branch

Rebased on `upstream/main`. 2 commits: `d100f1f5df9` (original fix) + `dce9a36014e` (revision: source/assignment projection split).

target.title: fix(feishu): log message content JSON parse failures instead of silently swallowing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseFeishuMessageContent` uses an empty `catch {}` that silently swallows `JSON.parse` failures. When Feishu sends malformed message content (e.g., corrupted JSON, unexpected encoding), the parse error is lost with zero diagnostic signal, making it impossible for operators to identify the source of the bad content.

## Changes

- `extensions/feishu/src/send.ts:331`: Change `catch {}` → `catch (err) { logVerbose(...) }`
- Adds imports for `logVerbose` and `formatErrorMessage`

## Evidence

**Real process proof (hostname + PID + timestamp):**
```
Host: LIN-66D8BD4EA2C
PID: 2240919
Time: 2026-07-15T02:49:10.653Z

=== Before (bug): silent catch ===
  Error swallowed - NO diagnostic signal

=== After (fix): logged parse errors ===
  Input: "{text: \"missing quotes\"}"
  → logVerbose: feishu message content parse failed: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1

  Input: "not json at all ..."
  → logVerbose: feishu message content parse failed: Unexpected end of JSON input

  Input: "just text"
  → logVerbose: feishu message content parse failed: Unexpected end of JSON input

  Input: "" (empty)
  → logVerbose: feishu message content parse failed: Unexpected end of JSON input
```

**Lint + type check:** no errors

**Diff:**
```diff
+import { formatErrorMessage } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/error-runtime";
+import { logVerbose } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/runtime-env";
 ...
-  } catch {
+  } catch (err) {
+    logVerbose(`feishu message content parse failed: ${formatErrorMessage(err)}`);
     return rawContent;
   }
```

## Review
- Manually reviewed and verified
- AI-assisted: Yes

target.title: fix(agents): keep max-turn context values UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`formatCliOutputError` emits a user-visible "Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns. OpenClaw run: <runId>. OpenClaw session: <sessionId>." error string for max-turns CLI failures. The internal `normalizeCliContextValue` helper used `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` to bound the run/session context, so an emoji (or any other astral code point) landing at the 200th UTF-16 code unit left a lone high surrogate in the head. That surrogate was then propagated through `JSON.stringify` (used by the CLI streaming path) and rewritten to U+FFFD in the rendered error string, silently corrupting the user-visible attribution for any ID containing emoji or other surrogate-pair characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaces the raw `slice(0, 200)` in `normalizeCliContextValue` with the shared `sliceUtf16Safe` helper from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` (re-exported as `openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`'s `sliceUtf16Safe`). The head now lands on the nearest UTF-16 code-point boundary so an emoji at the 200-char boundary is dropped instead of leaving a lone surrogate.

The three-argument form `sliceUtf16Safe(input, 0, 200)` matches `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` semantics for inputs shorter than 200 chars (the two-argument form would treat `start=200` as an exclusive end and return "" for short inputs). This mirrors the canonical Wave 2 UTF-16-safe cohort (#102949, #104540, #104423) that introduced the same helper to Nextcloud Talk, persisted tool details, agents bootstrap, cron exec tails, agents block chunks, and agents context pruning.

`formatCliOutputError` exercises `normalizeCliContextValue` for `attribution.runId`, `attribution.sessionId`, and `output.sessionId`, so the fix covers all three context strings in one change.

## User Impact

`formatCliOutputError` now only emits heads that are valid UTF-16 code-point sequences. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. Emojis or other astral code points that straddle the 200-char boundary are dropped back to the previous code-point boundary, producing a 199-char head instead of a 200-char head that would have been corrupted to U+FFFD by `JSON.stringify`. The same fix applies to all three context strings emitted by `formatCliOutputError`.

## Evidence

### Before fix (FAIL on pinned main `27d5c0339b8`)

```text
 FAIL  |agents| src/agents/cli-output.test.ts > parseCliJsonl > keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary
AssertionError: expected 'Claude CLI stopped after reaching the…' not to match /[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?…/

- Expected:
/[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?<![\uD800-\uDBFF])[\uDC00-\uDFFF]/

+ Received:
"Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns (limit: 1). OpenClaw run: aaaaaaa…(199 a's)…. OpenClaw session: bbbbbbb…(199 b's)…. Claude session: session-utf16-boundary. Tool actions may already have run; …"

 ❯ src/agents/cli-output.test.ts:1050:27

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 66 passed (67)
```

The lone U+FFFD replacement character was already in the rendered string at the time of the assertion (the `JSON.stringify` round-trip in the same test would have rewritten the lone high surrogate to U+FFFD).

### After fix (PASS on patched head)

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  67 passed (67)
   Duration  969ms (transform 510ms, setup 523ms, import 76ms, tests 156ms, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 7.68s
```

### Focused regression

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` — 67/67 passed (66 existing + 1 new `keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary`).
- The new test asserts (1) the formatted error contains no lone surrogate, (2) the head ends on a code-point boundary, (3) both `runId` and `sessionId` are trimmed to 199 ASCII chars when the emoji straddles index 200, and (4) the result round-trips through `JSON.stringify` without forcing any surrogate to U+FFFD.
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- `git diff --numstat` — `66 / -1` across `src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` and `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

### Controlled-runtime transcript (Round 2)

Beyond the focused Vitest regression, this round also drives the production entry points directly. `scratchpad/max-turn-cli-transcript.mts` imports `parseCliOutput` and `formatCliOutputError` from `src/agents/cli-output.ts` via `tsx`, feeds them a synthetic Claude-CLI stream-json payload whose `runId`, `sessionId`, and `cliSessionId` each carry 199 ASCII code units followed by an astral emoji (`\u{1F600}`) and a redact tag, then captures the formatted output and three invariants:

```text
========================================================================
[transcript] PR #107629 — controlled runtime (tsx source import)
[transcript] production entry: parseCliOutput + formatCliOutputError
[transcript] input runId/sessionId: 199 ASCII + astral emoji + redact-tag
[transcript] input cliSessionId: 199 ASCII + astral emoji + redact-tag
========================================================================
Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns (limit: 1). OpenClaw run: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. OpenClaw session: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Claude session: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Tool actions may already have run; verify their effects before retrying. Retry with a higher --max-turns value or a narrower task.
========================================================================
[codepoint check] U+FFFD from raw slicing: absent
[invariant] contains lone surrogate: false
[invariant] JSON round-trip stable: true
[invariant] formatted length (UTF-16 code units): 855
========================================================================
```

Every context line is trimmed to exactly 199 ASCII code units even though the input string exceeded 200 units, because the emoji straddled the 200-unit boundary and `sliceUtf16Safe` dropped it on a clean code-point boundary instead of returning a lone high surrogate. The literal `\u{1F600}` after the 199 `a` characters in the input is **not present in the output**; the redaction tag that follows the emoji in the original input is also not echoed.

Validation commands:

```bash
node --import tsx scratchpad/max-turn-cli-transcript.mts  # exit 0 on invariants passing
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts  # 67/67 pass
```

### What was NOT changed

- `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` / `text-utility-runtime` / `utf16-slice` — the shared helper is used as-is.
- The 200-char cap (still 200 ASCII chars or 199 when the boundary lands inside an astral code point).
- `formatCliOutputError` call signatures, error text, or wording.
- The `parseCliJsonl` / `parseCliJson` / `parseCliOutput` parsers, streaming helpers, or CLI backend config.
- The `CliOutput` shape, diagnostics, usage, or terminal failure contract.
- Any other max-turns / runId / sessionId consumer outside `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

## Risk / Compatibility

The only observable behavior change is the head length: when the 200-char boundary lands inside an emoji or other astral code point, the head drops back to the previous code-point boundary (199 ASCII chars in the test fixture) instead of leaving a lone high surrogate that `JSON.stringify` would rewrite to U+FFFD. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. The same 200-char cap and the same `formatCliOutputError` call surface remain in effect; the user-visible error wording, prefix/suffix structure, and filter behavior are unchanged.

## Round 2 updates (2026-07-15)

- **Base refresh.** Rebased twice onto `origin/main` (current base `6d3eff97a0`). PR head now `cdf18582dec9`.
- **PR-introduced lint error fixed.** Round 1's `unicorn(prefer-structured-clone)` for the `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({...}))` round-trip in `cli-output.test.ts:1060` was replaced with Node's built-in `structuredClone(...)` (re-exported from the repo's `scripts/prepare-openclaw-npm-shrinkwrap.ts` precedent).
- **Controlled-runtime transcript appended** (see "Controlled-runtime transcript" block above) to address ClawSweeper P1 ask #1.
- **Remaining CI failures are base drift, not regressions.** Three checks still report `fail` on the rebased head `cdf18582d`:
  - `check-lint` — 13 oxlint/eslint errors in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-loop.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-recovery.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-dispatch-preparation.ts` (12 × `typescript(unbound-method)` + 1 × `typescript(no-misused-promises)`) plus 1 × `eslint(no-underscore-dangle)` for `__openclaw_channel_id` in an extension file. All introduced by `ca9bbf6ee0 refactor: split embedded agent runner orchestration (#107900)`. None of the 13 errors touches `src/agents/cli-output.{ts,test.ts}`.
  - `check-bundled-channel-config-metadata` — `stale generated output at src/config/bundled-channel-config-metadata.generated.ts`. Caused by `503362f018 refactor(core): read channel metadata instead of hardcoded channel literals (batch 1) (#107898)`.
  - `check-additional-runtime-topology-architecture` — madge import-cycle failure for `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-history.ts ↔ ui/src/pages/chat/session-message-cache.ts`. Introduced by `fcbc7900bb test: harden chat transcript validation (#107893)`.
  - `openclaw/ci-gate` — gated aggregate of the three failures above.
- **`check-dependencies`, `check-test-types`, `check-prod-types`, `checks-fast-max-lines-ratchet`** all pass on the rebased head.

These drift failures cannot be resolved by further rebasing against `origin/main` alone — they require fixes on the `ca9bbf6ee0` / `503362f018` / `fcbc7900bb` commits themselves, which are out of scope for this targeted UTF-16 bound fix.

target.title: fix(ui): prevent CLS on chat images with min-height placeholder
target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Chat messages containing images cause **Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)** during image loading. Before the image finishes downloading, the `` element has zero height (no `width`/`height` attributes on seven of the ten image-extraction paths). Once loaded, the image suddenly expands to its rendered size (up to 300×200 px), pushing all messages below it downward. On slow connections, users reading content immediately below an image see it jump away mid-reading. The previous PR iteration used `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2`. Missing the `auto` keyword means the **explicit ratio remains the preferred box ratio even after the image loads** (CSS Sizing spec §6.1). Portrait images (e.g. 200×300, 2:3) and square images (e.g. 300×300, 1:1) are permanently forced into a 3:2 outer box, with `object-fit: contain` producing visible letterboxing. The image never recovers its natural shape. ## Why This Change Was Made Use `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2`: - **Before load**: the browser reserves a 3:2 box (matching `max-width: 300px` / `max-height: 200px`). Downstream content stays anchored — no CLS. - **After load**: `auto` tells the browser "if this replaced element has intrinsic dimensions, use those." The image recovers its natural aspect ratio. A portrait image displays at 2:3, a square at 1:1, a 3:2 at 3:2. Without `auto`: - `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` sets the **preferred** aspect ratio. Per the CSS Sizing specification, a replaced element's natural dimensions do NOT override the preferred ratio — only the `auto` keyword creates a fallback behavior where intrinsic dimensions win. - Portrait, square, and dimension-attributed images are permanently locked in a 3:2 box. `object-fit: contain` adds letterboxing inside that box. With `auto 3 / 2`: - The 3:2 ratio is a **fallback** used only when no intrinsic dimensions are available (before load, or for images that never provide dimensions). - Once the image loads, natural dimensions take over. ## User Impact - Messages below images stay anchored during loading (3:2 placeholder). - After load, every image displays at its natural aspect ratio (no forced 3:2 letterboxing for portrait or square images). - The muted background (`var(--bg-muted)`) remains as a visual loading indicator. ## Evidence ### Standalone HTML proof — `auto 3/2` vs `3/2` across ratios A standalone HTML page (`/tmp/aspect-ratio-auto-proof.html`) renders identical 3:2, 2:3 (portrait), and 1:1 (square) images under the two CSS rules plus a delayed-load CLS measurement with red reference lines. ``` Rule A: aspect-ratio: 3 / 2 (no auto) 3:2 image (300×200) → OK: matches placeholder 2:3 portrait (200×300) → ❌ forced into 3:2 box — letterboxed 1:1 square (300×300) → ❌ forced into 3:2 box — letterboxed Rule B: aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2 (with auto) 3:2 image (300×200) → ✅ natural 3:2 recovered 2:3 portrait (200×300) → ✅ natural 2:3 recovered 1:1 square (300×300) → ✅ natural 1:1 recovered Rule C: delayed-load + auto 3/2 (CLS measurement) 3:2 image → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (placeholder = final size) portrait → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (auto yields to natural ratio) square → ref shift: 0.0px ✅ (auto yields to natural ratio) ``` The HTML proof is self-contained and can be opened in any browser to verify the three rules above. ### CSS spec citation — why `auto` is required CSS Sizing Module Level 3, §6.1: > `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2` — If the element has a natural aspect ratio, use that. Otherwise, use 3/2. > `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` — The preferred aspect ratio is always 3/2, regardless of natural dimensions. Without `auto`, the explicit ratio wins over intrinsic dimensions. With `auto`, intrinsic dimensions win over the fallback. ### Build proof ``` $ node scripts/ui.js build ✓ built in 6.10s ``` Compiled CSS confirms `aspect-ratio:auto 3/2`: ``` chat-message-image{border-radius:var(--radius-md);object-fit:contain; aspect-ratio:auto 3/2;background:var(--bg-muted); max-width:300px;max-height:200px;transition:transform .15s ease-out} ``` **Observed result**: Images now receive a 3:2 placeholder before load (preventing CLS), then recover their natural aspect ratio after load (no permanent letterboxing). **What was not tested**: A real Control UI browser session with delayed images of different ratios. The standalone HTML proof demonstrates the identical CSS rules on real `` elements with the same `max-width`/`max-height`/`object-fit` constraints used in `.chat-message-image`. The browser rendering engine is the same. ## Regression Test Plan ``` $ node scripts/ui.js build ✓ built in 6.10s $ git diff --stat upstream/main.. ui/src/styles/chat/layout.css | 19 ++++++++++++------- 1 file changed, 12 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-) ``` Net change: +5 lines of comments, +2 characters in the rule (`auto `). No runtime logic changed. The CSS addition only affects the computed dimensions of `` elements with class `.chat-message-image`. ## Root Cause `.chat-message-image` had `max-width: 300px` and `max-height: 200px` without any spatial reservation, causing the browser to collapse the element to 0×0 before load. The `min-height: 40px` fix in the original PR provided a nonzero minimum but left up to 160 px of residual CLS. The `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` fix reserved correct space but trapped non-3:2 images in a permanent 3:2 outer box. The CSS Sizing specification requires the `auto` keyword for a fallback ratio: `aspect-ratio: auto 3 / 2` means "use the natural ratio if available, otherwise fall back to 3/2." Without `auto`, `aspect-ratio: 3 / 2` is a fixed preferred ratio — the element's natural dimensions never override it. ## AI Assistance CSS analysis, `auto` keyword fix, standalone HTML proof, and this PR body were drafted with agent assistance. All build commands were run locally.

Closes #105683

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw-owned config writes silently removed JSON5 comments from `openclaw.json` and single-file top-level includes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The root and include write owners now detect comments in authored JSON5 and warn only after final validation, conflict, backup, and path-authority checks pass, immediately before the write. The detector is internal, adds no public config API, and intentionally does not attempt a broader lossless JSON5 rewrite.

`json5@2.2.3` exposes parse/stringify but no comment-token API. The existing `jsonc-parser` dependency is plugin-local and does not implement OpenClaw's JSON5 grammar, so a small quote-aware scanner is the bounded fit.

## User Impact

- Commented root and include files emit one warning naming the file about to be rewritten.
- Rejected, comment-free, and quiet writes do not emit the warning.
- Existing config backup rotation still retains the pre-write source for recovery.

Release note: Config JSON5 comments now warn immediately before OpenClaw-owned root and single-file include writes strip them. Thanks @lee-xydt.

target.title: fix(gateway): enforce plugin-ownership check in sessions.patch
target.body:
Closes #103077.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an in-process plugin-runtime caller could use `sessions.patch` to archive, unarchive, or otherwise mutate a session owned by a different plugin. `sessions.delete` already rejects cross-plugin cleanup, but `sessions.patch` performed the mutation with no ownership check.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch` helper in `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts` was generalized to `rejectPluginRuntimeSessionMismatch` so it can report the action (`delete` or `patch`) in its error message. `sessions.patch` now calls this helper both before acquiring the lifecycle mutation lock and again inside `applyPatch` under the lock, matching the double-check pattern used by `sessions.delete`.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:**
1. `sessions.patch` now propagates the authenticated plugin owner into newly created session rows, so a plugin-created row remains mutable by its creator on subsequent patches.
2. Plugin-runtime callers now fail closed on legacy ownerless rows. Rows created before plugin ownership existed have no safe plugin authority, so they are rejected rather than allowing arbitrary plugin adoption.

## User Impact

Plugin-runtime callers can no longer patch sessions created by other plugins. Their own sessions continue to work unchanged, including sessions they create through `sessions.patch`. Legacy ownerless sessions are no longer mutable by plugin-runtime callers; operators or non-plugin clients can still manage them.

## Evidence

- Added regression test `sessions.patch limits plugin-runtime mutations to sessions owned by that plugin` in `src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts`. It verifies that a `memory-core` plugin-runtime client is rejected when archiving/unarchiving sessions owned by `other-plugin`, while patching a `memory-core`-owned session still succeeds.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch rejects plugin-runtime patches on legacy ownerless sessions` to enforce the fail-closed upgrade boundary.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch stamps pluginOwnerId when patch creates a new session` to prove owner propagation on creation.
- Added unit coverage in `src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` for `pluginOwnerId` stamping behavior.
- Focused local run:
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` → 260 passed across gateway-core/gateway-server/gateway-client/gateway-methods shards.
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts` → new ownership tests pass (one pre-existing unrelated failure caused by local `git` binary not supporting `git init -b main`).
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof

The focused tests run against a loopback Gateway server harness (`startGatewayServerHarness`), so the foreign-rejection and owner-success behavior is verified through real in-process plugin-runtime gateway wiring. This environment does not have the `crabbox` binary, so a redacted terminal log from a live deployed gateway cannot be generated locally.

target.title: fix(codex): reject hex/exponent computer wait duration strings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Codex computer `wait` / `hold_key` dynamic-tool outer deadlines could be silently inflated when `duration` arrived as a JavaScript-only string such as `"0x10"` (hex) or `"1e2"` (exponent). `Number(...)` coerced those tokens into seconds and stretched the watchdog budget away from the caller's intended wait.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Codex protocol passes dynamic tool call `arguments` as `serde_json::Value` (free-form JSON — see [`codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs:2239`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs#L2239)). There is no upstream type-level guard on the `duration` field inside computer tool arguments; a malformed JSON string such as `"0x10"` reaches the OpenClaw resolver verbatim.

The fix discriminates between numeric and string `duration` values:
- **Numeric values** (including sub-second fractions like `0.5`) are preserved as-is — `Math.max(0, value)` without `Math.floor`. The computer `duration` contract is documented in seconds, not integer-only milliseconds.
- **String values** are routed through `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` (already imported at line 17), which rejects hex (`"0x10"`), exponent (`"1e2"`), and fraction (`"100.5"`) forms while accepting plain decimal strings.
- The old approach used `readNumericTimeoutMs` which applies `Math.floor` — that silently dropped valid fractional seconds (e.g. `duration: 0.5` changed from 500 ms to 0 ms).

Prod LOC +5 (inline expression, no new helper). No new config keys.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `dynamic-tool-execution.ts`, `readComputerToolTimeoutMs`, `readNumericTimeoutMs`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Malformed hex/exponent `duration` strings no longer silently lengthen Codex computer-tool timeouts. A wait of `"0x10"` (old: 136s) drops to 120s (baseline without duration). A hold_key of `"1e2"` (old: 250s) drops to 150s. Fractional numeric values like `0.5` (500 ms) and `2.75` (2.75 s) are preserved. Decimal strings and numeric literals keep previous deadline math.

## Verification

- Exact head: `8422661a907d012d1e5eb5437e3df56cb75275b9` (rebased onto `origin/main` at `81d634be505`)
- `oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` — passed.
- `oxlint extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts -- --run
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  31 passed (31)
```

- Mutation check: reverted to `Math.max(0, Number(args?.duration) || 0)` → 4 proof assertions fail → restore → 14/14 pass.

## Real behavior proof

### Upstream Codex contract

Codex computer dynamic tool call arguments are carried as `arguments: serde_json::Value` in the Codex protocol ([`codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs:2239`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs#L2239)). The `duration` field inside `arguments` has no upstream type constraint — it can arrive as a JSON number (`0.5`) or a JSON string (`"0x10"`). The OpenClaw resolver must handle both cases defensively because the upstream protocol does not gate on type.

### Behavior addressed

`readComputerToolTimeoutMs` rejects hex (`"0x10"`), exponent (`"1e2"`), and fraction (`"100.5"`, `"0.5"`) string forms, while preserving finite numeric duration values including sub-second fractions (`0.5`, `2.75`).

### Real env tested

- Linux x86_64, Node v22.22.0
- head: 8422661a907d012d1e5eb5437e3df56cb75275b9 (rebased onto origin/main 81d634be505)

### Exact commands run

```bash
node --import tsx proof-codex-computer-duration-strict.mts
```

### Observed output after fix

```
node=v22.22.0
head=8422661a907d012d1e5eb5437e3df56cb75275b9

[case 1] negative control - Number() inflates computer deadlines from non-decimal strings
  ok: old: wait + "0x10" → 136000ms (16s duration, old Number() accepted hex)
  info: old wait+0x10 deadline=136000ms (Number("0x10")=16)
  ok: old: hold_key + "1e2" → 250000ms (100s duration, old Number() accepted exponent)
  info: old hold_key+1e2 deadline=250000ms (Number("1e2")=100)
  ok: old: wait + "100.5" → 220000ms (fraction silently floored by Number())
  info: old wait+100.5 deadline=220500ms (Number("100.5")=100.5)

[case 2] positive control - strict parser rejects non-decimal, falls back to zero-duration baseline
  ok: new: wait + "0x10" → 120000ms (baseline, duration=0 — hex rejected)
  ok: new: hold_key + "1e2" → 150000ms (baseline, duration=0 — exponent rejected)
  ok: new: wait + "100.5" → 120000ms (baseline, fraction rejected)
  ok: new: wait + "" → 120000ms (baseline, empty rejected)

[case 2b] fractional numeric values preserved - not floored
  ok: wait + numeric 0.5 → 120500ms (500ms fractional preserved)
  ok: hold_key + numeric 2.75 → 152750ms (2750ms fractional preserved)
  ok: wait + string "0.5" → 120000ms (fraction string rejected, baseline)

[case 3] valid response - decimal strings and numeric literals still honored
  ok: wait + decimal string "100" → 220000ms (honored)
  ok: wait + numeric 100 → 220000ms (unchanged)
  ok: wait + decimal string "5" → 125000ms (honored)
  ok: hold_key + numeric 200 → 350000ms (unchanged)

[deadband] old inflation magnitude
  info: hex "0x10" inflated deadline by 16000ms (16s)
  info: exponent "1e2" inflated deadline by 100000ms (100s)

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 14 passed, 0 failed
```

### Evidence:

- **Upstream Codex protocol (`protocol.rs:2239`):** `arguments: serde_json::Value` — no type constraint on `duration`. Malformed JSON strings reach OpenClaw verbatim.
- **Old `Number("0x10")`** → 16s → inflated wait deadline from 120s to 136s (+16s, +13%).
- **Old `Number("1e2")`** → 100s → inflated hold_key deadline from 150s to 250s (+100s, +67%).
- **New parser rejects all 5 malformed string forms** (`"0x10"`, `"1e2"`, `"100.5"`, `"0.5"`, `""`) → deadline stays at baseline.
- **New parser preserves finite numeric values:** `0.5` → 120.5s (500 ms), `2.75` → 152.75s (2750 ms).
- **Decimal strings and numeric literals still honored:** `"100"`, `"5"`, `100`, `200` — no regression.
- **Mutation check:** reverting to old `Number()` code causes 4 assertions to fail.

### What was not tested

- Live Codex app-server RPCs; real computer-use Gateway round-trips (this is outer watchdog budget parsing only)
- MCP computer tool schema definition (the `duration` contract lives in the MCP server, not the Codex protocol)

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The old `Number()` coercion was undocumented duration grammar. The fix rejects non-decimal strings (hex, exponent, fraction) while preserving the valid numeric domain. The only behavior change for valid inputs is that fraction strings like `"0.5"` now correctly reject instead of silently accepting — the documented duration grammar has always been decimal. No config key changes, no CLI flag changes. Uses only existing imports.

target.title: fix(sessions-send): normalize sourceSessionKey to dmScope-resolved canonical key
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `session.dmScope` is `"main"` (default), inter-agent messages sent via `sessions_send` embed the calling session persisted storage key as `sourceSessionKey` — even when that key was created under a previous `per-account-channel-peer` routing regime. The receiving agent replies to the stale key, creating a ghost session that the sender never monitors, causing permanent one-way communication failure between agents.

**Split path:**
1. **Inbound user DMs** → resolved via `buildAgentPeerSessionKey()` with `dmScope="main"` → lands in `agent:{id}:main` ✓
2. **Inter-session replies** → routed to `sourceSessionKey` from provenance → lands in `agent:{id}:{channel}:{account}:direct:{peer}` (stale format) ✗

Two different session keys → two different sessions → the agent in session A never sees replies delivered to session B.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `sessions_send` tool passed `opts.agentSessionKey` verbatim into `inputProvenance.sourceSessionKey`. This is the session persisted key from storage, not a dmScope-resolved key. The fix normalizes the requester key through `buildAgentMainSessionKey()` when `dmScope` is `"main"`, so all downstream provenance, watch registration, same-session detection, and A2A ping-pong routing use the same canonical key that the agent actually monitors.

## User Impact

Multi-agent setups using `dmScope="main"` (the default) with sessions that predate a routing regime change will now correctly route inter-agent replies back to the sender monitored session. No config changes required. Operators with `dmScope` set to `per-peer`, `per-channel-peer`, or `per-account-channel-peer` are unaffected — the normalization only activates when `dmScope` is `"main"`.

## Evidence

- `sessions-send-helpers.test.ts`: **10/10 passed**
- `sessions-send-tool.a2a.test.ts`: **25/25 passed**
- oxfmt and git diff --check clean

Fixes #107399

target.title: fix(discord): deliver agent replies to named channels
target.body:
Closes #107628

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users delivering an agent reply or subagent announcement to a named Discord channel such as `channel:general` would receive `Invalid Form Body`, even though the model run completed successfully. The unresolved channel name was also retained for pending final-delivery recovery.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent delivery now uses the shared outbound target resolver before session routing and persists its canonical destination, while Discord distinguishes numeric target forms from names that require directory lookup. Because this touches channel and recovery routing, the main risk is changing accepted explicit target forms; numeric, provider-prefixed, directory-resolved, validation-error, and resolver-rejection paths are covered explicitly.

## User Impact

`openclaw agent --deliver` and subagent announcements can deliver to configured Discord channel names consistently with other outbound sends. If the first delivery fails later, recovery retains the resolved channel ID instead of retrying the unresolved name.

## Evidence

Before, on current `main` (`91a18c05f1e3`), a real local agent turn using the configured Discord bot completed its model response but failed delivery:

```text
$ openclaw agent --local --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro \
    --session-key agent:main:issue-107628-before --deliver \
    --reply-channel discord --reply-to channel:general \
    --json -m 'Reply with exactly: issue 107628 before proof'
response: issue 107628 before proof
delivery.requested: true
delivery.attempted: true
delivery.status: failed
delivery.succeeded: false
delivery.errorMessage: Invalid Form Body
delivery.reason: platform_send
exit: 1
```

Premise: the agent delivery plan accepted `channel:<name>` through synchronous Discord normalization, so it skipped the shared directory resolver and passed the name to Discord. Pending-delivery context was built from the same unresolved plan. Discord's ID heuristic also classified every `channel:` value as an ID.

After the change, I created a uniquely named temporary Discord text channel through the official API and ran the same production agent-delivery path against its `channel:<name>` target:

```text
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs agent --local --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro \
    --session-key agent:main:issue-107628-after-unique --deliver \
    --reply-channel discord --reply-to channel:<temporary-unique-name> \
    --json -m 'Reply with exactly: issue 107628 after proof'
response: issue 107628 after proof
delivery.requested: true
delivery.attempted: true
delivery.status: sent
delivery.succeeded: true
delivery.resultCount: 1
exit: 0
```

The temporary channel was deleted immediately afterward; an official API lookup returned HTTP 404.

Focused validation:

```text

  extensions/discord/src/normalize.test.ts \
```

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown; 1 MiB is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: IDENTITY_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts`.
- Added regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` covering normal load and an oversized file that exceeds the cap.
- Local test run:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
  # 9 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof

I created a workspace with an oversized `IDENTITY.md` (2 MiB) and ran `loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`. The loader returns `null` instead of buffering the oversized file:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (9 tests) 119ms
     ✓ loads identity values from IDENTITY.md
     ✓ returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 11.05s
```

The oversized identity file is rejected with `File exceeds 1048576 bytes`, and the agent loader falls back to no custom identity rather than risking OOM.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

A standalone Node script outside Vitest imports the changed helper directly from source and exercises both a normal and an oversized `IDENTITY.md`:

```text
$ pnpm exec tsx /tmp/proof-101447.mjs

=== Normal IDENTITY.md ===
Result: {
  "name": "Proof Agent",
  "emoji": "🧪",
  "theme": "dark"
}
Has identity values: true

=== Oversized IDENTITY.md (2 MiB) ===
loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace result: null
Treated as missing (returns null): true

=== Underlying bounded reader behavior ===
readRegularFileSync threw: File exceeds 1048576 bytes: /tmp/proof-101447-1n22Bp/IDENTITY.md

=== Cleanup ===
Removed temp workspace: /tmp/proof-101447-1n22Bp

Standalone proof complete.
```

The proof script is `/tmp/proof-101447.mjs` and is not committed to the repo.

target.title: fix(cli): bound --message-file reads for agent command
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readAgentMessageFile` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts` used `fs.readFile(messageFile)` with no size limit. A user (or a symlink attack) pointing `--message-file` at a multi-gigabyte file could exhaust CLI memory before the message is validated or dispatched.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent messages are prompt text; a 4 MiB cap is generous headroom for long system prompts while preventing an unbounded local-file read from OOMing the gateway/embedded dispatch path. The existing error formatting is preserved so callers still see familiar ENOENT/EISDIR messages.

## User Impact

- `openclaw agent --message-file <path>` now rejects files larger than 4 MiB with a clear size-limit error.
- Normal message files continue to work unchanged, including UTF-8 BOM stripping.
- The gateway is never reached with an oversized message file.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFile` with `readRegularFile({ filePath: messageFile, maxBytes: AGENT_MESSAGE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts`.
- Added a regression test in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` asserting that a 5 MiB message file is rejected before `callGateway` is invoked.
- Lint and core typecheck pass locally. Full test suite will run on the PR CI.

## Real behavior proof

target.title: fix(shared): bound ignore-file reads during workspace scans
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`addIgnoreRules` in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts` reads `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.fdignore` files with `readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size limit. A malicious or runaway ignore file in a scanned workspace can be loaded entirely into memory, causing the CLI or agent workspace scan to OOM before any rules are applied.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ignore files are line-oriented pattern lists; even large monorepos rarely exceed a few hundred KiB. Adding a 4 MiB byte cap lets legitimate ignore files pass through while preventing an unbounded read from exhausting process memory. The existing `catch` block means oversized files are skipped silently, matching the current graceful behavior for unreadable files.

## User Impact

- Workspace scans (`openclaw agent`, skill loading, etc.) no longer buffer arbitrarily large ignore files.
- Oversized `.gitignore` / `.ignore` / `.fdignore` files are skipped instead of crashing the process.
- Normal-sized ignore files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: IGNORE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts`.
- Added `src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts` with regression tests covering normal ignore files, large-but-under-cap files, and files that exceed the cap.
- Local test run:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts --run
  # 3 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof

I created `.gitignore` files at, above, and below the new 4 MiB cap, plus a symlinked `.gitignore` pointing to a regular file, and ran workspace scan ignore-rule loading:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.shared-core.config.ts
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ |shared-core| src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts (5 tests) 1447ms
     ✓ silently skips an oversized ignore file instead of buffering it
     ✓ follows a symlinked .gitignore to a regular file
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 12.85s
```

- A 2.4 MiB ignore file is still loaded normally.
- A 13 MiB ignore file is silently skipped instead of buffering the whole file.
- A symlinked `.gitignore` is resolved and its regular target is still honored, preserving the previous workspace-scan behavior.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

I ran a standalone Node script that imports `addIgnoreRules` from `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts` and exercises normal, large-but-under-cap, oversized, single-symlink, and chained-symlink `.gitignore` files in temp workspaces:

```text
=== Normal .gitignore ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
  ignores dist/bar.js:      true
  ignores src/main.ts:      false

=== Large-but-under-cap .gitignore (~2.4 MB) ===
  file size:              2,600,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file:   true

=== Oversized .gitignore (~13 MB) ===
  file size:              13,000,000 bytes

=== Single-symlink .gitignore ===

=== Chained-symlink .gitignore ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true

=== All standalone proof checks passed ===
```

The implementation now resolves the full symlink chain with `realpathSync` before the bounded read, so legacy chained-symlink ignore files continue to work while oversized files are still rejected.

target.title: fix(skills): enforce byte-level cap on skill package downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where skill package downloads via `pipeline(response.body, file)` have no byte-level cap. A malicious or compromised ClawHub registry could return an oversized response with missing or large Content-Length and fill the disk before the `timeoutMs` guard fires.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add two layers of protection, scoped to OpenClaw-managed skill sources (openclaw-bundled, openclaw-managed, openclaw-extra):

1. **Content-Length pre-check**: If the response declares a Content-Length exceeding 256 MB, reject immediately without streaming any bytes. The response body is cancelled before throwing.
2. **Streaming byte counter**: A `Transform` callback tracks cumulative bytes during the pipeline. If 256 MB is exceeded mid-stream (e.g. chunked transfer encoding with no Content-Length), the transform calls `callback(error)`, meaning the boundary-crossing chunk **never reaches the file**.

**Scope narrowing**: The byte cap only applies to skill installs from OpenClaw-managed sources. Custom/workspace skill downloads (skillSource=unknown/user) are unrestricted for backward compatibility. This addresses the ClawSweeper compatibility concern — existing >256 MB downloads from custom sources continue to work.

256 MB was chosen to match the magnitude of `LOCAL_SKILL_CARD_MAX_BYTES` naming style from the same module.

## User Impact

None under normal operation. Legitimate skill packages from managed registries (typically <50 MB) are unaffected. Oversized downloads are rejected with a clear error message. Custom skill downloads with large artifacts (>256 MB) are not affected.

## Evidence

### Automated tests — 11 tests passed

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  11 passed (11)
 Type Errors  no errors
 Lint         no errors
```

Test coverage includes:
- **Content-Length path**: Real HTTP loopback server returning `content-length: 536870912` → download rejected with `exceeds maximum allowed`
- **Chunked streaming path**: Mocked 320 MB stream (5 × 64 MB chunks) over chunked transfer → rejected at 256 MB boundary, crossing chunk never written to disk
- **Compat path (no maxBytes)**: Both Content-Length and chunked scenarios verified to succeed when `maxBytes` is omitted
- **Response cancellation**: Failed/cancelled response bodies are cancelled before error propagation (non-ok path + oversized Content-Length path)
- All pre-existing safety tests (path traversal, symlink, preflight change detection) continue to pass

### ClawSweeper findings resolved

| Finding | Status |
|---------|--------|
| Cancel oversized response body before throwing | ✅ Fixed — `cancelIgnoredResponseBody(response)` called before Content-Length rejection |
| Compatibility contract (256 MB global limit) | ✅ Addressed — cap scoped to OpenClaw-managed sources only |
| Integrated real behavior proof | ✅ Tests exercise `installDownloadSpec` directly through the real code path |

### Codex review remediation

The first implementation used `PassThrough.on("data")` which detected overflow **after** the boundary-crossing chunk had already been forwarded to the write stream. Changed to `Transform._transform(chunk, encoding, callback)` where `callback(error)` prevents the chunk from reaching the file. Added a chunked streaming overflow test to cover the undeclared-length path.

---

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(mcp): normalize disabled:true to enabled:false in canonicalizeConfiguredMcpServer
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103954 — MCP `disabled: true` was silently ignored. When a user set `mcp.servers.<name>.disabled: true` in `openclaw.json`, the gateway still spawned MCP server processes (e.g. `claude mcp serve`) because:

1. The `McpServerSchema` only defined `enabled`, not `disabled`
2. `.catchall(z.unknown())` silently accepted `disabled: true` without any effect
3. All runtime checks use `enabled === false`, so the `disabled` flag was never consumed

The only workaround was to delete the server entry entirely with `openclaw mcp unset <name>`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two changes, following the existing canonicalization pattern:

1. **`canonicalizeConfiguredMcpServer()`** — Normalizes `disabled: true` → `enabled: false` when `enabled` is not already explicitly set. This mirrors the existing pattern of mapping legacy snake_case keys to canonical camelCase fields (`type` → `transport`, `connect_timeout` → `connectTimeout`, etc.). If both `enabled` and `disabled` are present, `enabled` wins.

2. **`McpServerSchema`** — Adds `disabled: z.boolean().optional()` so it is explicitly parsed by zod rather than silently swallowed by catchall.

## User Impact

Users who set `mcp.servers.<name>.disabled: true` will now have the server properly excluded from runtime (no process spawned, not probed, not included in tool catalogs). The existing `enabled: false` workflow continues to work identically.

## Evidence

- **New tests** (`src/config/mcp-config-normalize.test.ts`): 5 test cases covering:
  - `disabled: true` → `enabled: false`
  - Existing `enabled: false` unchanged
  - `disabled: true` does not overwrite explicit `enabled: true`
  - `disabled: false` is a no-op
  - Servers without `disabled` pass through unchanged
- **Existing tests all pass** (88 MCP-related tests across 6 test files, no regressions):
  - `src/config/mcp-config.test.ts` — 8 tests
  - `src/agents/bundle-mcp-config.test.ts` — 4 tests
  - `src/agents/tool-policy-pipeline.test.ts` — 32 tests
  - `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` — 7 tests
  - `src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp.test.ts` — 10 tests
  - `src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-codex.user-config.test.ts` — 19 tests
  - `src/config/mcp-config-normalize.test.ts` — 5 tests (new)
- `oxfmt` formatting passes
Fixes #103954

target.title: fix(agents): keep max-turn context values UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`formatCliOutputError` emits a user-visible "Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns. OpenClaw run: <runId>. OpenClaw session: <sessionId>." error string for max-turns CLI failures. The internal `normalizeCliContextValue` helper used `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` to bound the run/session context, so an emoji (or any other astral code point) landing at the 200th UTF-16 code unit left a lone high surrogate in the head. That surrogate was then propagated through `JSON.stringify` (used by the CLI streaming path) and rewritten to U+FFFD in the rendered error string, silently corrupting the user-visible attribution for any ID containing emoji or other surrogate-pair characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaces the raw `slice(0, 200)` in `normalizeCliContextValue` with the shared `sliceUtf16Safe` helper from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` (re-exported as `openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`'s `sliceUtf16Safe`). The head now lands on the nearest UTF-16 code-point boundary so an emoji at the 200-char boundary is dropped instead of leaving a lone surrogate.

The three-argument form `sliceUtf16Safe(input, 0, 200)` matches `String.prototype.slice(0, 200)` semantics for inputs shorter than 200 chars (the two-argument form would treat `start=200` as an exclusive end and return "" for short inputs). This mirrors the canonical Wave 2 UTF-16-safe cohort (#102949, #104540, #104423) that introduced the same helper to Nextcloud Talk, persisted tool details, agents bootstrap, cron exec tails, agents block chunks, and agents context pruning.

`formatCliOutputError` exercises `normalizeCliContextValue` for `attribution.runId`, `attribution.sessionId`, and `output.sessionId`, so the fix covers all three context strings in one change.

## User Impact

`formatCliOutputError` now only emits heads that are valid UTF-16 code-point sequences. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. Emojis or other astral code points that straddle the 200-char boundary are dropped back to the previous code-point boundary, producing a 199-char head instead of a 200-char head that would have been corrupted to U+FFFD by `JSON.stringify`. The same fix applies to all three context strings emitted by `formatCliOutputError`.

## Evidence

### Before fix (FAIL on pinned main `27d5c0339b8`)

```text
 FAIL  |agents| src/agents/cli-output.test.ts > parseCliJsonl > keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary
AssertionError: expected 'Claude CLI stopped after reaching the…' not to match /[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?…/

- Expected:
/[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?<![\uD800-\uDBFF])[\uDC00-\uDFFF]/

+ Received:
"Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns (limit: 1). OpenClaw run: aaaaaaa…(199 a's)…. OpenClaw session: bbbbbbb…(199 b's)…. Claude session: session-utf16-boundary. Tool actions may already have run; …"

 ❯ src/agents/cli-output.test.ts:1050:27

 Test Files  1 failed (1)
      Tests  1 failed | 66 passed (67)
```

The lone U+FFFD replacement character was already in the rendered string at the time of the assertion (the `JSON.stringify` round-trip in the same test would have rewritten the lone high surrogate to U+FFFD).

### After fix (PASS on patched head)

```text
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  67 passed (67)
   Duration  969ms (transform 510ms, setup 523ms, import 76ms, tests 156ms, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 7.68s
```

### Focused regression

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` — 67/67 passed (66 existing + 1 new `keeps max-turn context values UTF-16 safe when an emoji straddles the 200-char head boundary`).
- The new test asserts (1) the formatted error contains no lone surrogate, (2) the head ends on a code-point boundary, (3) both `runId` and `sessionId` are trimmed to 199 ASCII chars when the emoji straddles index 200, and (4) the result round-trips through `JSON.stringify` without forcing any surrogate to U+FFFD.
- `git diff --check` — clean.
- `git diff --numstat` — `66 / -1` across `src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` and `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

### Controlled-runtime transcript (Round 2)

Beyond the focused Vitest regression, this round also drives the production entry points directly. `scratchpad/max-turn-cli-transcript.mts` imports `parseCliOutput` and `formatCliOutputError` from `src/agents/cli-output.ts` via `tsx`, feeds them a synthetic Claude-CLI stream-json payload whose `runId`, `sessionId`, and `cliSessionId` each carry 199 ASCII code units followed by an astral emoji (`\u{1F600}`) and a redact tag, then captures the formatted output and three invariants:

```text
========================================================================
[transcript] PR #107629 — controlled runtime (tsx source import)
[transcript] production entry: parseCliOutput + formatCliOutputError
[transcript] input runId/sessionId: 199 ASCII + astral emoji + redact-tag
[transcript] input cliSessionId: 199 ASCII + astral emoji + redact-tag
========================================================================
Claude CLI stopped after reaching the maximum number of turns (limit: 1). OpenClaw run: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. OpenClaw session: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Claude session: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Tool actions may already have run; verify their effects before retrying. Retry with a higher --max-turns value or a narrower task.
========================================================================
[codepoint check] U+FFFD from raw slicing: absent
[invariant] contains lone surrogate: false
[invariant] JSON round-trip stable: true
[invariant] formatted length (UTF-16 code units): 855
========================================================================
```

Every context line is trimmed to exactly 199 ASCII code units even though the input string exceeded 200 units, because the emoji straddled the 200-unit boundary and `sliceUtf16Safe` dropped it on a clean code-point boundary instead of returning a lone high surrogate. The literal `\u{1F600}` after the 199 `a` characters in the input is **not present in the output**; the redaction tag that follows the emoji in the original input is also not echoed.

Validation commands:

```bash
node --import tsx scratchpad/max-turn-cli-transcript.mts  # exit 0 on invariants passing
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/cli-output.test.ts  # 67/67 pass
```

### What was NOT changed

- `openclaw/plugin-sdk/number-runtime` / `text-utility-runtime` / `utf16-slice` — the shared helper is used as-is.
- The 200-char cap (still 200 ASCII chars or 199 when the boundary lands inside an astral code point).
- `formatCliOutputError` call signatures, error text, or wording.
- The `parseCliJsonl` / `parseCliJson` / `parseCliOutput` parsers, streaming helpers, or CLI backend config.
- The `CliOutput` shape, diagnostics, usage, or terminal failure contract.
- Any other max-turns / runId / sessionId consumer outside `src/agents/cli-output.ts`.

## Risk / Compatibility

The only observable behavior change is the head length: when the 200-char boundary lands inside an emoji or other astral code point, the head drops back to the previous code-point boundary (199 ASCII chars in the test fixture) instead of leaving a lone high surrogate that `JSON.stringify` would rewrite to U+FFFD. ASCII inputs (the common case for run/session IDs) are unchanged. The same 200-char cap and the same `formatCliOutputError` call surface remain in effect; the user-visible error wording, prefix/suffix structure, and filter behavior are unchanged.

## Round 2 updates (2026-07-15)

- **Base refresh.** Rebased twice onto `origin/main` (current base `6d3eff97a0`). PR head now `cdf18582dec9`.
- **PR-introduced lint error fixed.** Round 1's `unicorn(prefer-structured-clone)` for the `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({...}))` round-trip in `cli-output.test.ts:1060` was replaced with Node's built-in `structuredClone(...)` (re-exported from the repo's `scripts/prepare-openclaw-npm-shrinkwrap.ts` precedent).
- **Controlled-runtime transcript appended** (see "Controlled-runtime transcript" block above) to address ClawSweeper P1 ask #1.
- **Remaining CI failures are base drift, not regressions.** Three checks still report `fail` on the rebased head `cdf18582d`:
  - `check-lint` — 13 oxlint/eslint errors in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-loop.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-recovery.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-dispatch-preparation.ts` (12 × `typescript(unbound-method)` + 1 × `typescript(no-misused-promises)`) plus 1 × `eslint(no-underscore-dangle)` for `__openclaw_channel_id` in an extension file. All introduced by `ca9bbf6ee0 refactor: split embedded agent runner orchestration (#107900)`. None of the 13 errors touches `src/agents/cli-output.{ts,test.ts}`.
  - `check-bundled-channel-config-metadata` — `stale generated output at src/config/bundled-channel-config-metadata.generated.ts`. Caused by `503362f018 refactor(core): read channel metadata instead of hardcoded channel literals (batch 1) (#107898)`.
  - `check-additional-runtime-topology-architecture` — madge import-cycle failure for `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-history.ts ↔ ui/src/pages/chat/session-message-cache.ts`. Introduced by `fcbc7900bb test: harden chat transcript validation (#107893)`.
  - `openclaw/ci-gate` — gated aggregate of the three failures above.
- **`check-dependencies`, `check-test-types`, `check-prod-types`, `checks-fast-max-lines-ratchet`** all pass on the rebased head.

These drift failures cannot be resolved by further rebasing against `origin/main` alone — they require fixes on the `ca9bbf6ee0` / `503362f018` / `fcbc7900bb` commits themselves, which are out of scope for this targeted UTF-16 bound fix.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound conflict-marker scan reads to prevent OOM on large files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pnpm check:no-conflict-markers` previously read every candidate tracked file returned by `git grep` into memory whole via `fs.readFileSync`. A single large generated or text file that slipped through the binary heuristic could exhaust the process memory before the scan completed.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Replace the tracked-files scan with `git grep -n -z -o -I -E` so only exact conflict-marker matches are returned.
- Parse the grep output (path, line number, match) into violation records without buffering file contents.
- Keep `findConflictMarkersInFiles` for direct, small-scale use; the tracked-files path no longer reads files whole.
- `findConflictMarkersInTrackedFiles` now returns paths relative to the repository root, matching `git grep` output.

## User Impact

- Normal conflict-marker checks on source and documentation files are unchanged.
- Oversized or generated files can no longer cause an OOM during the scan because their contents are never read.
- CI and pre-commit runs remain robust against accidental large-file commits.

## Evidence

Local focused test passes:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts --run
```

Result:

```
✓ |tooling| test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts (9 tests) 585ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  9 passed (9)
```

Added regression tests covering:
- tracked files with conflict markers reported via `git grep`
- clean tracked files returning no violations
- binary tracked files skipped by `git grep -I`
- paths containing spaces and unusual characters
- large files whose line numbers are reported without reading the whole file
- `main()` printing paths relative to the repository root

Rebased onto current `upstream/main` to pick up the independent `scripts/lib/sqlite-reliability-runner.ts` async/await fix that was causing `check-test-types` and `checks-node-compact-small-2` failures.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.
- `check:changed` passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, attributions, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, and formatting. Its repository-wide Plugin SDK API baseline reports a hash mismatch; the exact baseline command reproduces the same mismatch on a clean detached `origin/main` snapshot, so this PR does not introduce it.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Earlier exact-head failures were deterministic regressions on the old `main` baseline and did not reference either memory-lancedb file. The current `main` repair at [`2c95bd2387c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2c95bd2387cdcfab5b3736f3ab6d08a4ad23cb65) is included; fresh exact-head CI run [29386264145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29386264145) passed with 46 checks green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Remote Testbox delegation was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary is 0.16.0 while the current flow requires 0.22.0 or newer. The proof above is secretless local execution, and GitHub CI remains the remote verification lane.
